newsitem.title: USA: U.S House blocks debate on emergency spending bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S House blocks debate on emergency spending bill.

text.p: The House blocked debate Wednesday on an emergency spending bill providing $8.4 billion to help weather-ravaged states and fund U.S. military operations, as lawmakers rebelled over a host of contentious add-ons.
In a setback for Republican leaders, the House voted 193-229 on a rule needed to open debate on the aid bill, which has been mired in partisan bickering over issues great and small.
House leaders later appeared ready to drop some controversial amendments in an effort to get the bill moving.
"We're going to write a new rule, come back tomorrow, bring this up and pass it," said House Majority Whip Tom DeLay, one of 43 Republicans who voted no.
The emergency spending bill contains $5.5 billion to aid more than 30 states struggling to recover from severe storms and flooding.
Issues delaying the bill ranged from policy in Bosnia to nutrition aid to a regional fight over whether to increase the number of companies supplying paper for U.S. currency.

Republican leaders said they would likely drop an amendment that would have cut off funding for U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia after June 30, 1998. The bill provides nearly $2 billion for these activities and continued U.S. military flights in the Gulf.
The White House had threatened a veto if the amendment passed. Democrats opposed it and Republicans were divided.
Republicans were having second thoughts about their plan to provide $76 million for a special nutrition programme for poor women and children.

Some Republicans voted against the rule because it automatically provided the full $76 million the White House requested for the Women, Infants and Children programme -- doubling the amount in the bill.
On the other side, Democrats, only 13 of whom voted for the rule, were angry because their party was prevented from offering a separate WIC amendment.

Another problem was a regional fight over changing the current system for producing paper for U.S. currency. The paper is now produced by one Massachusetts company. Lawmakers from other states, including DeLay of Texas, want firms in their region to have a shot.

Clinton also strongly objects to an amendment to continue federal programmes automatically if the White House and Congress did not pass needed spending bills. It is not clear what will happen to that plan.
"We were concerned about automatic funding," said Minnesota Democrat Bruce Vento. "Some Republicans were trying to embarrass the president on Bosnia."
The Senate last week passed its version of the spending bill after a long, messy debate. Clinton has threatened to veto the Senate measure because it contains the automatic spending authority.

Disputes over spending forced two government shutdowns in fiscal year 1996, and polls show the public blames the shutdowns on Republicans. Supporters of the automatic spending plan say it is simply a good government insurance policy to prevent future closures.
The White House says the plan would take the pressure off lawmakers and provides a lower level of spending than Republicans have promised for Clinton's domestic priorities.
